Module 1 — Module Organizer (Student Word Doc): Build Spec

Build note (teacher/builder): This spec describes the single Microsoft Word document each student keeps for the whole module — the Module Organizer. Students create it at module start (Lesson 1.01), save it in OneDrive under English 1 → Module 1, and return to it every week for notes, vocabulary, character tracking, reflection, recitation, and their evolving essay thesis. Produce it as a clean, branded `.docx` template (navy/cyan headings, Segoe UI) with the sections and fillable spaces below. Nothing in the Organizer is auto-graded; it is the student's working notebook and is checked biweekly via the Reading Journal / Organizer Check (completion). Keep instructions short; the students do the filling.

File name for students: `Organizer_LastName_FirstName`

Header block (top of doc)

  • Course line: ENGLISH 1 · 9th Grade ELA · Module 1: Justice in Greek Tragedy — Electra by Sophocles
  • Student name / date fields.
  • Owl glyph consistent with course chrome (optional, decorative only).

Section 1 — The Central Question (top, always visible)

A boxed callout at the very top the student can never scroll past:

What is justice — what is owed to the gods, the city (polis), and the family?

Below it, one line: "Everything in this Organizer is here to help you answer this question by the end of the module."

Section 2 — Word Study / Vocabulary (fill in weekly)

A table the student adds to each week from that week's reading. Pre-seed Week 1's terms; leave blank rows for Weeks 2–5.

WordWhat it means (in your words)Where it appears / how it's usedWord origin or word family
justice
duty
polis
piety
(add weekly: vengeance, anagnorisis, catharsis, dramatic irony, …)

Note under the table: "You must use at least three of these terms in each Quick Write and in your module essay — so keep this current."

Section 3 — Character Tracking Chart

A table the student updates at every reading (the module's spine assessment; submitted at the milestones noted in the weekly plans). Columns exactly:

CharacterRole in the playStance on justice (what do they think is owed, and to whom?)Key lines / notes (with speaker & moment)

Instruction line: "Add to this chart every time you read. By Week 5 it becomes a map of every position on justice in the play — and a quarry for essay evidence."

Section 4 — Weekly Notes & Reflection

One repeating block per week (Weeks 1–5), each with:

  • This week I read: (structural landmark, e.g., "the Prologue" / "Electra vs. Chrysothemis")
  • What I noticed about justice this week: (2–3 sentences)
  • A line worth keeping: (short quote + speaker & moment)
  • A question I still have: (1 sentence)

Section 5 — Recitation

A short boxed section (plum accent) for the module's recitation piece:

  • Piece I chose: (title / passage and speaker)
  • Why I chose it: (1–2 sentences)
  • Practice notes: (dates practiced, lines that are hard, delivery reminders — pacing, emotion, looking up)

Line: "You will submit a recorded recitation for this module (device-agnostic). Use this space to plan and track your practice."

Section 6 — Evolving Thesis (the essay grows here all module)

A running space the student revisits after each Quick Write, so the essay position develops over five weeks:

  • After Week 1 (Quick Write 1) — my first take on what is owed:
  • After Week 2 — how the sisters' argument changed my thinking:
  • After Week 3 — Clytaemnestra vs. Electra; who has the better claim to justice?
  • After Week 4 — after the revenge, do I think justice was done?
  • Week 5 — MY WORKING THESIS for the essay: (one arguable sentence)
  • Three pieces of evidence I will use (speaker & moment):

Module 2 — Module Organizer (Student Word Doc): Build Spec

Build note (teacher/builder): This spec describes the single Microsoft Word document each student keeps for the whole module — the Module Organizer. Students create it at module start (Lesson 1.01), save it in OneDrive under English 1 → Module 2, and return to it every week for notes, vocabulary, character tracking, the disputatio prewriting, recitation, and their evolving argument. Produce it as a clean, branded `.docx` template (navy/cyan headings, Segoe UI) with the sections and fillable spaces below. Nothing in the Organizer is auto-graded; it is the student's working notebook and is checked biweekly via the Reading Journal / Organizer Check (completion). Keep instructions short; the students do the filling.

File name for students: `Organizer_LastName_FirstName`

Header block (top of doc)

  • Course line: ENGLISH 1 · 9th Grade ELA · Module 2: Honor and Duty — Sir Gawain and the Green Knight by the Pearl Poet
  • Student name / date fields.
  • Owl glyph consistent with course chrome (optional, decorative only).

Section 1 — The Central Question (top, always visible)

A boxed callout at the very top the student can never scroll past:

What does it mean to be truly honorable, and what does it reveal about us when we fall short?

Below it, one line: "Everything in this Organizer is here to help you answer this question, and to build toward your disputatio essay: Is Gawain a man of honor?"

Section 2 — Word Study / Vocabulary (fill in weekly)

A table the student adds to each week from that week's reading. Pre-seed all five weeks' terms in the first column (grouped by week as below); students fill the remaining columns as each week arrives.

WeekWordWhat it means (in your words)Where it appears / how it's usedWord origin or word family
1chivalry
1covenant
1churlish
1imperious
1appease
2piety
2manifold
2mien
2surpassing
2inviolate
3beguile
3wily
3assay
3peril
3largesse
4execration
4dissemble
4remiss
4notorious
4indignant
5epitome
5concession
5refutation
5equivocation
5exemplar

Note under the table: "You must use at least three of these terms in each Quick Write and in your module essay, so keep this current. Copia practice: each week, take one sentence from the reading that contains a vocabulary word and rewrite it three ways — substitute a synonym, alter the syntax, and change the register."

Section 3 — Character Tracking Chart

A table the student updates at every reading (the module's spine assessment; submitted at the milestones noted in the weekly plans). Columns exactly:

CharacterRole in the poemStance on honor (what do they think honor requires, and do they meet it?)Key lines / notes (with speaker & moment, cite by Fitt)
Sir Gawain
King Arthur
Queen Guinevere
The Green Knight / Bertilak of Hautdesert
Lady Bertilak
Morgan le Fay
The guide to the Green Chapel

Instruction line: "Add to this chart every time you read. By Week 5 it becomes a map of every position on honor in the poem, and a quarry for evidence in your objections, your response, and your replies."

Section 4 — Weekly Notes & Reflection

One repeating block per week (Weeks 1–5), each with:

  • This week I read: (structural landmark, e.g., "Fitt I: the feast and the Green Knight's challenge")
  • What I noticed about honor this week: (2–3 sentences)
  • A line worth keeping: (short quote + speaker & moment, cite by Fitt)
  • A question I still have: (1 sentence)

Section 5 — Disputatio Graphic Organizer (the heart of the prewriting)

The scholastic disputation form structures the whole essay. Fill each row as evidence accumulates across the weeks; by Week 5 this table becomes your outline. Present as a two-column table (Section / Prompt on the left, generous fillable space on the right).

SectionPromptYour notes
Disputed QuestionWhat is the moral question being argued?Is Gawain a man of honor?
Objection 1State, in its strongest and fairest form, one real reason someone would say Gawain is not a man of honor.
Objection 2State a second fair reason someone would deny his honor.
Objection 3 (optional)A third fair objection, if you use one.
On the Contrary (sed contra)Name one line or structural observation from the poem (or the chivalric tradition) that grounds the case for his honor. Quote it.
I Answer That (respondeo)State your own reasoned answer to the question. Begin with what a man of honor is, then judge Gawain against it, drawing on all four Fitts.
Reply to Objection 1Why is the first objection incomplete or mistaken? Answer it directly and fairly.
Reply to Objection 2Why is the second objection incomplete or mistaken?
Reply to Objection 3 (optional)Answer the third objection, if used.

Note under the table: "An objection you can knock over easily is not worth stating. State each objection so well that its own supporters would nod, then answer it. That is intellectual honesty, and it is graded."

Section 6 — Recitation

A short boxed section (indigo accent) for the module's recitation piece:

  • Passage I chose: (lines and speaker, cite by Fitt)
  • Why I chose it: (1–2 sentences)
  • Practice notes: (dates practiced, alliterative lines that are hard to say aloud, delivery reminders — pacing, stress on the alliterating sounds, looking up)

Line: "You will submit a recorded recitation for this module (device-agnostic). Use this space to plan and track your practice, and listen for the alliterative beat as you rehearse."

Section 7 — Evolving Argument (the essay grows here all module, rung by rung)

A running space the student revisits after each weekly rung, so the disputatio develops over five weeks:

  • After Week 1 (Rung 1: Alliterative catalog) — a first alliterative description I could reuse as my opening paragraph:
  • After Week 2 (Rung 2: Virtue catalog) — what the pentangle demands, and where Gawain already looks strong or shaky:
  • After Week 3 (Rung 3: Ethopoeia) — writing in Lady Bertilak's voice showed me this about the temptation, and it gives me Objection ___:
  • After Week 4 (Rung 4: Essay opening + objections) — my thesis (does Gawain have honor?) and my two strongest objections:
  • Week 5 (Rung 5: Final essay) — MY WORKING THESIS: (one arguable sentence answering Is Gawain a man of honor?)
  • Three pieces of evidence I will use, one from each of at least three different Fitts (quote + speaker & moment):

1.

Closing line: "When you reach Week 5, your disputatio is already half-written. Each rung filled one part of it, from the alliterative opening to the replies."

Module 3 — Module Organizer (Student Word Doc): Build Spec

Build note (teacher/builder): This spec describes the single Microsoft Word document each student keeps for the whole module — the Module Organizer. Students create it at module start (Lesson 1.01), save it in OneDrive under English 1 → Module 3, and return to it every week for notes, vocabulary, character tracking, copia practice, recitation, and their evolving thesis. Produce it as a clean, branded `.docx` template (navy/cyan headings, Segoe UI) with the sections and fillable spaces below. Nothing in the Organizer is auto-graded; it is the student's working notebook and is checked biweekly via the Reading Journal / Organizer Check (completion). Keep instructions short; the students do the filling.

File name for students: `Organizer_LastName_FirstName`

Header block (top of doc)

  • Course line: ENGLISH 1 · 9th Grade ELA · Module 3: The Character of a Traveler — The Canterbury Tales by Geoffrey Chaucer
  • Student name / date fields.
  • Owl glyph consistent with course chrome (optional, decorative only).

Section 1 — The Central Question (top, always visible)

A boxed callout at the very top the student can never scroll past:

What does the character of a traveler reveal about their soul?

Below it, one line: "Everything in this Organizer is here to help you answer this question, and to build toward your module project: The Pilgrim's Portrait, an essay arguing which pilgrim best embodies or most betrays one of the seven Optima virtues."

Section 2 — Word Study / Vocabulary (fill in weekly)

A table the student adds to each week from that week's reading. Pre-seed all five weeks' terms in the first columns (grouped by week as below); students fill the remaining columns as each week arrives. These are the exact terms from the module scope.

Section 3 — Weekly Copia Practice (the vocabulary workout)

A short repeating block, one per week (Weeks 1–5). Copia means richness: you rewrite one sentence many ways to stretch your control of language.

For each week:

  • The sentence I chose (with one Word Study term in it):
  • Rewrite 1 — substitute a synonym:
  • Rewrite 2 — expand the phrase (add detail without changing the meaning):
  • Rewrite 3 — imitate the syntax with new content (keep the shape, change the subject):

Line under the block: "Take one sentence from the week's reading that contains a vocabulary word and rewrite it three ways. This is how a word becomes yours, not just a definition you memorized."

Section 4 — Character Tracking Chart (the module's spine)

A table the student updates at every reading. This chart is the direct engine of the Pilgrim's Portrait: by Week 5 it holds every pilgrim you could write about and the evidence to do it. Columns exactly:

Instruction line: "Add to this chart every time you read. Watch for the gap between what a pilgrim claims and what the details reveal. That gap is where Chaucer hides his judgment, and where your best evidence will come from. By Week 5 this chart becomes a map of every soul on the road to Canterbury, and the quarry for your Pilgrim's Portrait."

Section 5 — Weekly Notes & Reflection

One repeating block per week (Weeks 1–5), each with:

  • This week I read: (structural landmark, e.g., "General Prologue, lines 1–42, and the portraits of the Knight and the Wife of Bath")
  • What I noticed about character and soul this week: (2–3 sentences)
  • A line worth keeping: (short quote in Middle English + a modern gloss + speaker/moment, cite by line)
  • A question I still have: (1 sentence)

Section 6 — Recitation

A short boxed section (indigo accent) for the module's recitation piece:

  • Passage: the opening of the General Prologue in Middle English ("Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote...", General Prologue, lines 1–18). Recite it in the original Middle English.
  • My pronunciation notes: (mark the words that sound different from modern English: soote, licour, Zephirus, croppes, halwes, corages; note where final -e is sounded)
  • Practice notes: (dates practiced, lines that are hard to say aloud, delivery reminders — pacing, the spring rhythm, looking up)

Line: "You will submit a recorded recitation of the General Prologue opening in Middle English (device-agnostic). Use this space to plan and track your practice. Read it aloud until the strange spelling turns back into music. This is a Tier-3 showcase for the module, so rehearse it like a performance."

Section 7 — Evolving Thesis (the essay grows here, step by step)

A running space the student revisits after each of the five weekly project steps, so the Pilgrim's Portrait develops over the module. Each step is one Quick Write feeder.

  • After Step 1 (Quick Write 1: The Modern Pilgrim) — a modern traveler I described through telling details, and what that taught me about reading Chaucer's method:
  • After Step 2 (Quick Write 2: What the Tale Reveals) — a claim about how a teller's chosen tale exposes the teller (Knight vs. Miller), and the pilgrim I am starting to circle for my essay:
  • After Step 3 (Quick Write 3: Comedy's Argument) — what Chaucer argues about human nature through comedy, and which virtue or vice this points me toward:
  • After Step 4 (Quick Write 4: Inside and Outside the Voice) — writing in a pilgrim's voice and then judging it from the outside showed me this about the gap between self-presentation and character:
  • Step 5 (Quick Write 5: The Thesis Takes Shape) — MY WORKING THESIS: (one arguable sentence naming one pilgrim and one Optima virtue, and claiming that this pilgrim best embodies or most betrays it)
  • The strongest counterargument to my thesis, stated fairly (the best case someone could make against my reading):
  • Three pieces of textual evidence I will quote (MLA), from the portrait and/or the tale (quote + cite by line):

Module 4 — Module Organizer (Student Word Doc): Build Spec

Build note (teacher/builder): This spec describes the single Microsoft Word document each student keeps for the whole module — the Module Organizer. Students create it at module start (Lesson 1.01), save it in OneDrive under Optima → ELA → ELA9 → Module 4, and return to it every week for notes, vocabulary, the sonnet-form reference, their growing draft, recitation practice, and craft-statement notes. Produce it as a clean, branded `.docx` template (navy/cyan headings, Segoe UI) with the sections and fillable spaces below. Nothing in the Organizer is auto-graded; it is the student's working notebook and is checked via the module's completion check. Keep instructions short; the students do the filling.

File name for students: `Organizer_LastName_FirstName`

Header block (top of doc)

  • Course line: ENGLISH 1 · 9th Grade ELA · Module 4: Love, Time, and the Sonnet — Sonnets 18, 29, 116, and 130 by William Shakespeare
  • Student name / date fields.
  • Owl glyph consistent with course chrome (optional, decorative only).

Section 1 — The Central Question (top, always visible)

A boxed callout at the very top the student can never scroll past:

What can fourteen lines hold? What does a sonnet reveal about love, time, and human dignity?

Below it, one line: "Everything in this Organizer is here to help you answer this question, and to build toward your own original sonnet: fourteen lines that argue."

Section 2 — Word Study / Vocabulary (fill in weekly)

A table the student adds to each week from that week's lessons. Pre-seed all three weeks' terms in the first column (grouped by week as below); students fill the remaining columns as each week arrives.

WeekWordWhat it means (in your words)Where it appears / how it's usedWord origin or word family

1apostrophe
1temperate
2anaphora
2blazon
2haply
2parody

3doom
3alter

Note under the table: "You will use this vocabulary in your quizzes, your discussion post, and above all your craft statement, so keep it current. Copia practice: each week, take one sentence from a lesson that contains a vocabulary word and rewrite it three ways — substitute a synonym, alter the syntax, and change the register."

Section 3 — The Sonnet Form: Reference Map (pre-filled reference, plus blanks to confirm)

A boxed reference table showing the Shakespearean rhyme-scheme map. Pre-fill the structure columns; leave the "job" column partly blank for the student to complete during Week 1.

LinesUnitRhymeThe unit's job in the argument
1–4Quatrain 1A B A B(student fills: opens the claim…)
5–8Quatrain 2C D C D(student fills: deepens or complicates…)
9–12Quatrain 3E F E F(student fills: the turn usually lands here…)
13–14CoupletG G(student fills: the verdict…)

Below the table, three short reference lines:

  • Meter: iambic pentameter — ten syllables, five da-DUM beats per line.
  • Volta: pivot word + a genuine change in what the speaker knows or sees. Home position is line 9; Sonnet 116 turns early (line 5) and Sonnet 130 late (line 13), both on purpose.
  • Contrast note (fill in Week 1): how the Petrarchan form divides its fourteen lines differently: _______________

Section 4 — Weekly Notes & Reflection

One repeating block per week (Weeks 1–3), each with:

  • This week I read: (e.g., "Sonnet 18: the summer's day promise")

  • A question I still have: (1 sentence)

Section 5 — Drafting Space (keyed to the three project feeders)

The project grows here, feeder by feeder. Present as three labeled blocks with generous fillable space:

After Feeder 1 (Week 1 — three lines in iambic pentameter):

  • My subject: _______________

After Feeder 2 (Week 2 — first quatrain):

After Feeder 3 (Week 3 — full draft, all 14 lines):

  • My volta: pivot word _____ at line _____ ; what changes there: _______________
  • My couplet: verdict or summary? Be honest, then note the fix if needed: _______________
  • Stumble list from reading aloud (lines to revise for the final): _______________

Closing line: "When you reach the final project, your sonnet is already drafted and your craft statement is already half-written. Each feeder filled one part of it."

Section 6 — Recitation Showcase (chosen sonnet + practice log)

A short boxed section (indigo accent) for the semester's Tier-3 Recitation Showcase:

  • Why I chose it: (1–2 sentences)

DateWhat I practiced (lines/quatrains)What still trips me

Line: "You will submit a recorded, from-memory recitation of your chosen sonnet (device-agnostic: Canvas recorder, phone, or your VR platform). A couplet a day is all it takes. Use this log so your practice is visible to you."

Section 7 — Craft Statement Notes (the paragraph grows here)

A running space the student revisits after each week, so the craft statement is assembled before it is written:

  • My volta: line _____ , pivot word _____ ; what the speaker knows or sees after it that they could not say before: _______________
  • One deliberate variation (metrical or a broken parallel), if any, and why: _______________

The House of Atreus: Mapping a Family Curse
Solo VR Activity · 10 pts · completion
🌟 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
Electra's family carries a curse that began generations before she was born. Today you will build a visual family tree of that curse in your VR space, then record yourself explaining how this bloody history changes the way you read the play's opening. The generations of wrong that came before are exactly why Electra feels justice is owed.
🛠 WHAT YOU NEED
Your VR headset and workspace, with whatever tools it gives you for placing boards, notes, or drawings in the space. No headset today? You may build the same family tree in a drawing or slides app instead. The thinking is what counts, not the device.
THE HOUSE OF ATREUS · FIVE GENERATIONS, EACH ANSWERING BLOOD WITH BLOOD
Tantalus
tests the gods, is cursed
↓

↓
Atreus

📜 THE CURSE OF THE HOUSE OF ATREUS
The curse begins with Tantalus, who in his arrogance kills his own son and serves him to the gods to test them. The gods punish the whole bloodline. His descendants Atreus and Thyestes feud for the throne of Mycenae; Atreus takes a monstrous revenge by killing Thyestes' sons and serving them to him at a feast. Thyestes' surviving son, Aegisthus, is raised to avenge that wrong. Atreus's son Agamemnon becomes king and leads the Greeks to Troy, but to sail, he sacrifices his own daughter, Iphigenia. While he is at war, his wife Clytaemnestra, grieving Iphigenia and allied with Aegisthus, murders Agamemnon on his return. Their surviving children are Electra and Orestes, where our play begins. Every generation answered blood with blood, each certain a debt was owed.

3

A catalog is a description that builds by piling up detail after detail in a steady, parallel rhythm. Week 5 · You are here
Rungs 1 through 4 are the work already done: your Alliterative catalog, your Virtue catalog, your Ethopoeia, and your Essay opening with objections. This final rung assembles them into one polished disputatio.
📖 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
You have read the Pearl Poet’s Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and asked, all module long, what it means to be truly honorable and what it reveals about us when we fall short. Now you argue the question in the form the medieval schools used to test hard cases: the disputatio. You state the question, raise the strongest objections against your own answer, ground your case in the poem, reason it through across all four Fitts, and then answer each objection in turn. Everything you have built points here: your alliterative catalog, your virtue catalog, your ethopoeia, and your essay opening with its objections.
✎ THE DISPUTED QUESTION
Is Gawain a man of honor?
Take a position and defend it. Gawain keeps his word to seek the Green Chapel, endures three temptations, and then hides the green girdle and calls himself a coward. Does one failure undo a life of virtue, or does honor include how a man answers for his fall? Argue from the text.
📝 REQUIRED STRUCTURE — THE DISPUTATIO, IN ORDER
1
Alliterative opening paragraph. Open in imitation of the Pearl Poet’s catalog style (6 to 8 lines), using alliterative pairs and parallel structure. This is your Rung 1 catalog, revised.
2
Thesis. End the opening with one clear sentence that directly answers the question: is Gawain a man of honor?
3
Objectiones. State at least two objections to your thesis, each in its strongest and fairest form. An objection you can knock over easily is not worth stating.
4
Sed contra. Offer one line from the poem or one structural observation that grounds the case for your side. Quote it and name where it appears.
5
Respondeo. Give your reasoned answer in 4 to 6 paragraphs, drawing evidence from all four Fitts. Begin with what honor is, then judge Gawain against it.
6
Replies to objections. Answer each objection you raised, one at a time, fairly and specifically. Target length for the whole essay: 750 to 1,000 words.
✅ ALSO REQUIRED
☐
Quote the poem accurately and introduce each quotation in your own words. Cite by speaker and moment and by Fitt, not by a page number.
☐
Use at least three module Word Study terms accurately (for example chivalry, covenant, piety, largesse, dissemble, refutation).
☐
Proofread once more before you submit. This is the one teacher-graded assessment of the module.
📚 THE TEXT
Draw your evidence from the free, public-domain Jessie Weston translation (1898): d.lib.rochester.edu/camelot/text/weston-sir-gawain-and-the-green-knight.html. Every quotation you use must be a real line from the text that you can point to by Fitt and moment.

☐ Submit the _Final file through Canvas using the OneDrive tab.

📋 HOW YOUR DISPUTATIO WILL BE SCORED
Your teacher looks at four things. Read this before you draft: it tells you exactly what a strong disputatio does.
Criterion Strong Developing Beginning
Understanding of the text Draws accurate, well-chosen evidence from all four Fitts; reads the poem’s parallel scenes and the girdle closely, not just its plot. Uses some accurate evidence, but it clusters in one or two Fitts, or leans on summary. Retells the story or misreads key moments; little real evidence from the text.
Quality of reasoning Defines honor, judges Gawain against it, and carries the respondeo across 4 to 6 paragraphs; each reply genuinely answers its objection. Reasons in places, but the respondeo is thin, or a reply repeats the thesis instead of answering the objection. Asserts a verdict without reasoning; objections go unanswered or the structure is missing.
Clarity and precision Alliterative opening lands; disputatio sections are clearly marked and ordered; sentences are varied; at least three Word Study terms used well; nearly error-free. Generally clear; the opening or the section order is uneven, or fewer than three terms are used well; some errors. Hard to follow; sections blur together; frequent errors interfere with meaning.
Intellectual honesty States each objection so fairly its own supporters would agree, then answers it; concedes what is true in the other side without abandoning the thesis. Objections are stated, but weakly, or set up only to be dismissed; little real concession. Objections are strawmen or absent; the argument ignores the strongest case against it.
🎤 OPTIONAL: PRESENT YOUR ARGUMENT (COMPLETION ADD-ON)
You may also present your disputatio out loud as a short oral or visual argument: a 3 to 5 minute recording in which you state your thesis, walk through your strongest objection and your reply to it, and read your alliterative opening aloud. RECITATION SHOWCASE · SEMESTER 1 OF THE SPRING TERM'S ORAL TRADITION
Recite the General Prologue
The famous opening, in Chaucer's own Middle English — the words readers have spoken aloud for six hundred years
🎤 YOUR SHOWCASE
This is the big one: your Recitation Showcase for the semester. For six centuries, students have carried the opening of the General Prologue in their memories, and this module you join them. Recite lines 1 through 18 ("Whan that Aprille…" through "…whan that they were seeke") in Middle English, from memory if you can, or read expressively if that suits you better. Memory earns the highest marks on one criterion, but an expressive, well-prepared reading is a strong performance too. Nobody expects perfect fourteenth-century pronunciation. What we are listening for is care: that you know what you are saying, that the rhythm carries you, and that the lines sound alive. Start rehearsing now; it is due at the end of the module, and a few lines a day is all it takes.
📚 YOUR PASSAGE · THE OPENING 18 LINES
THE GENERAL PROLOGUE, LINES 1–18 (MIDDLE ENGLISH, PUBLIC DOMAIN)
Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote
The droghte of March hath perced to the roote,
And bathed every veyne in swich licour
Of which vertu engendred is the flour;
Whan Zephirus eek with his sweete breeth
Inspired hath in every holt and heeth
The tendre croppes, and the yonge sonne
Hath in the Ram his halfe cours yronne,
And smale foweles maken melodye,
That slepen al the nyght with open ye
(So priketh hem Nature in hir corages),
Thanne longen folk to goon on pilgrimages,
And palmeres for to seken straunge strondes,
To ferne halwes, kowthe in sondry londes;
And specially, from every shires ende
Of Engelond, to Caunterbury they wende,
The hooly blisful martir for to seke,
That hem hath holpen whan that they were seeke.
Modern gloss: When April with its sweet showers has pierced the drought of March to the root, and bathed every vein of the plants in the moisture whose power brings forth the flower; when the west wind too, with his sweet breath, has breathed life into the tender shoots in every wood and field, and the young sun has run half its course through the sign of the Ram, and small birds make melody who sleep all night with open eyes (so Nature stirs them in their hearts), then people long to go on pilgrimages, and pilgrims to seek far-off shores and distant shrines known in various lands; and especially, from every shire's end of England, they travel to Canterbury to seek the holy blessed martyr who helped them when they were sick.
🗣️ HOW TO SOUND LIKE CHAUCER (CLOSE ENOUGH)
Middle English says more of its letters than we do. Three habits get you most of the way there:
1. Sound every syllable. Final -e is often pronounced as a soft "uh": soote is "SAW-tuh," roote is "ROH-tuh." That extra syllable keeps the ten-beat rhythm.
2. Vowels are "continental," as in Spanish or Italian. Aprille is "ah-PRIL-luh," melodye is "meh-loh-DEE-uh," licour is "lee-COOR."
3. Say the consonants you see. The k in knyght and the gh (a soft throat sound, like German "ach") are both spoken: "k-nicht."
When in doubt, keep the beat. The five-beat line will carry you through any uncertain vowel.
📝 HOW TO PREPARE (A LITTLE EACH DAY BEATS A LOT AT ONCE)
1
Read the gloss first so you know exactly what every line means. You cannot perform what you do not understand.
2
Learn it in chunks of two lines (one rhyming couplet at a time). The rhymes are your memory hooks: soote/roote, licour/flour, breeth/heeth.
3
Rehearse aloud, tapping the five beats in each line. Save your biggest breath for the turn at line 12: Thanne longen folk to goon on pilgrimages. That is the line the whole sentence has been waiting for.
4
Record in one take when you are ready. A small stumble is fine: recover and keep going, the way a live performer would.
🎥 RECORD IT — YOUR CHOICE OF TOOL
Record audio or video however is easiest for you:
☐ the Canvas media recorder built into this assignment, or
☐ your phone (then upload the file), or
☐ your VR platform's recording tool (then upload).
Any of these is accepted equally. Say your name at the start, and say whether you are reciting from memory or reading.
📊 HOW YOUR SHOWCASE IS GRADED (4 CRITERIA)
CriterionA strong performance…
Accuracy & memorizationDelivers all 18 lines with the words right, in order, with nothing skipped. From memory earns the top of this criterion; an accurate expressive reading still earns solid credit here.
Middle English pronunciationShows real effort with the three habits above: sounded final -e, continental vowels, spoken consonants. Consistent effort matters more than scholarly perfection.
Pace & clarityEvery word is audible and unhurried; the five-beat rhythm is steady; the recording is clear enough to follow line by line.
ExpressionThe lines sound understood, not chanted: spring feels alive, the long build gathers, and the arrival at "Thanne longen folk…" lands like the turn it is.
Your teacher scores each criterion on the Canvas rubric attached to this assignment and leaves brief feedback. Prepare with the four rows above in front of you and you know exactly what is being listened for.
📤 HOW TO SUBMIT
Submit your recording to this Canvas assignment (upload the file or use the built-in media recorder). Then add one line to the "Recitation" note in your Module Organizer: the line you are proudest of, and why.

📖 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
You have read Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales in the original Middle English and asked, all module long, what the character of a traveler reveals about their soul. Now you make the argument in writing. Choose one pilgrim from the road to Canterbury. Choose one of the seven Optima virtues. Then argue, from the text, that this pilgrim best embodies that virtue or most betrays it. Your Character Tracking Chart already holds the pilgrims and the evidence; your thesis from Quick Write 5 is your starting line. This essay is where the portrait comes into focus.
✎ THE PROMPT
Which Canterbury pilgrim best embodies, or most betrays, one of the seven Optima virtues?
The seven virtues are courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. Pick one pilgrim and one virtue, and take a clear position: does this pilgrim live the virtue out, or expose it by falling short? Remember Chaucer’s method. He rarely states a judgment; he lets a telling detail do the work. Your strongest evidence often lives in the gap between what a pilgrim claims and what the portrait or tale quietly reveals.
Eligible pilgrims include the Knight, the Prioress, the Miller, the Wife of Bath, the Nun’s Priest, the Pardoner, and the Franklin. Ask your teacher before writing on a pilgrim outside this list.

Introduction and thesis. Introduce your pilgrim and briefly situate them in the pilgrimage. End the paragraph with one clear sentence that names the pilgrim, names the virtue, and states whether they embody it or betray it. This is your thesis from Quick Write 5, revised.

Body: your case. In three or more paragraphs, build your argument. Each paragraph should make one claim, quote the text, and explain how the quotation proves your point. Draw from both the General Prologue portrait and the pilgrim’s tale where you can.
3

At least three pieces of textual evidence, quoted directly from Chaucer and formatted in MLA style. Introduce each quotation in your own words, then explain it. Quote the Middle English accurately; you may add a brief modern gloss in brackets.

RECITATION SHOWCASE · SEMESTER 2 OF THE YEAR'S ORAL TRADITION
The Sonnet Showcase: Recite Shakespeare from Memory
Fourteen lines that readers have carried in their heads for four hundred years. This module, you carry one too.
🎤 YOUR SHOWCASE
This is the big one: your Recitation Showcase for the semester, the companion to the Middle English lines you performed for Chaucer. Choose one of the module's four sonnets (18, 29, 116, or 130), learn it by heart, and recite all fourteen lines from memory, recorded. Before you recite, introduce the poem in one sentence of your own words: what the sonnet argues. That single sentence tells your teacher you are not just repeating sounds; you know what you are saying. A sonnet is a friendly memorization task: the rhymes are hooks, the meter is a current, and fourteen lines is a couplet a day for a week. Start early, rehearse a little daily, and by the end of the week the poem will be yours for life. Nobody expects a flawless studio take. What we are listening for is care: the right words, a steady pace, and lines that sound understood.
📚 CHOOSE YOUR SONNET · FOUR POEMS, FOUR TEMPERAMENTS
SONNET 18 · THE PROMISE
"Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?"
Warm, confident, famous. The steady build from question to promise makes it one of the friendliest to memorize.
SONNET 29 · THE RESCUE
"When, in disgrace with Fortune and men's eyes"
Dark to bright in fourteen lines. The volta at "Yet" is the most dramatic turn of the four; a gift to an expressive performer.
SONNET 116 · THE DEFINITION
"Let me not to the marriage of true minds"
An argument you can lean on: negation, star, sickle, wager. If you can follow the logic, the lines follow the logic.
SONNET 130 · THE WINK
"My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun"
The comic option, with a straight face required until line 13. Timing is everything; the couplet must land like a punchline that turns sincere.
All four poems are public domain. The full texts are in your module lessons, and the complete 1609 collection is free at Project Gutenberg (Shakespeare's Sonnets, eBook #1041). Record your choice in the Recitation section of your Module Organizer.
📝 HOW TO PREPARE (A LITTLE EACH DAY BEATS A LOT AT ONCE)
1
Understand it first. Reread your lesson notes and write, in your Organizer, the one-sentence introduction you will speak: what the sonnet argues. You cannot perform what you do not understand, and this sentence is graded.
2
Learn it quatrain by quatrain, two lines at a time. The rhyme scheme is your memory map: every A calls its A, every B calls its B. Say the lines aloud from the start; silent memorizing does not survive a recording.
3
Rehearse with the beat: tap the five stresses in each line. Find the volta and let your voice mark it; the turn is where an audience leans in, and it is where your Expression score is won.
4
Record in one take when you are ready. A small stumble is fine: recover and keep going, the way a live performer would. Log each practice day in your Organizer's recitation table.
🎥 RECORD IT — YOUR CHOICE OF TOOL
Record audio or video however is easiest for you:
☐ the Canvas media recorder built into this assignment, or
☐ your phone (then upload the file), or
☐ your VR platform's recording tool, in any location you choose (then upload).
Any of these is accepted equally. Say your name, name your sonnet, give your one-sentence introduction, then recite from memory: no paper, no screen with the text on it.
📊 HOW YOUR SHOWCASE IS GRADED (4 CRITERIA)
Your teacher listens for four things. Rehearse with these four rows in front of you and you know exactly what is being listened for.
Criterion Strong Developing Beginning
Memorization & accuracy All fourteen lines from memory, words right and in order; a small self-corrected slip does not break the performance. Mostly from memory, with a few dropped or substituted words, or a line recovered out of order. Large portions missing, invented, or read rather than recited.
Pace & clarity Every word audible and unhurried; the five-beat line is steady without turning sing-song; the recording is easy to follow. Generally clear, but rushed or mumbled in stretches, or the rhythm wobbles enough to lose lines. Hard to hear or follow; the pace swallows whole phrases.
Expression & interpretation The lines sound understood, not chanted: the volta lands audibly, and the couplet is delivered like the verdict it is. Some phrasing shows understanding, but the delivery flattens; the turn passes without being heard. A monotone recitation of syllables; nothing in the voice marks what the lines mean.
Understanding (the one-sentence intro) One clear sentence, in the student's own words, that accurately names what the sonnet argues. An intro is given but stays vague ("it is about love") or partly misreads the poem. No introduction, or a sentence that shows the poem was not understood.
Your teacher scores each criterion on the Canvas rubric attached to this assignment and leaves brief feedback.

📖 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
For three weeks you have read Shakespeare's sonnets from the inside: the fourteen-line frame, the quatrains that argue, the volta that turns, the couplet that risks. Now you finish your own. Take your Feeder 3 draft, revise the lines your ear flagged, and submit a finished Shakespearean sonnet on your chosen subject, together with a short craft statement that defends your decisions and your recorded performance of the poem. Everything you have built this module points here.
✎ THE TASK
Write an original Shakespearean sonnet that makes one clear argument about a subject you actually care about.
The subject is yours: a person, a place, a fear, a season, a question. What is not optional is the arguing. Shakespeare's sonnets do not merely describe; they claim something and earn it across three quatrains. Yours should too, and your couplet should do more than wave goodbye.
📝 REQUIRED ELEMENTS — ALL SIX, IN ONE SUBMISSION
1
Fourteen lines of iambic pentameter. Ten syllables per line, five da-DUM beats, with natural word stress. A deliberate variation for emphasis is welcome if your craft statement can name it.
2
The Shakespearean rhyme scheme: ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. Real rhymes throughout; one near-rhyme is acceptable if it is a choice, not an escape.
3
A deliberate volta. A pivot word plus a genuine change in what the speaker knows, sees, or feels. Line 9 is the home position; turn earlier or later only on purpose, the way Sonnet 116 turns at line 5.
4
A couplet that delivers a verdict. The last two lines must do something the poem could not have done at line 1: judge, wager, concede, or turn to the reader. Not a summary.
5
A craft statement (one paragraph, about 5 to 8 sentences) below the poem. It must state what your sonnet argues, name two techniques you used deliberately (with the line numbers where they appear) and why you chose them, and say where your volta falls and what changes there. Use the module's craft vocabulary accurately: quatrain, couplet, volta, iambic pentameter, and the technique names themselves.
6
Your recorded performance. Attach the recording from Performance Practice 3, or a fresh take of the finished poem: all fourteen lines, a one-beat pause at the volta, ending with the spoken sentence "My sonnet argues that…" Any recording tool is accepted (Canvas recorder, phone, or your VR platform).
✅ BEFORE YOU SUBMIT
☐

☐
Read the finished poem aloud once more (or let Word's Read Aloud do it). If you stumble, your reader will too.
☐
Proofread the craft statement. This is the one teacher-graded writing assessment of the module; make it easy to admire.
📚 YOUR MODELS
Sonnets 18, 29, 116, and 130 are your four blueprints: a promise, a rescue, a definition, a wink. All are public domain; the full texts are in your module lessons, and the complete 1609 collection is free at Project Gutenberg (eBook #1041). Imitate their moves, not their words: the argument, the turn, and the couplet that risks something are the inheritance you are claiming.
📁 M365 SKILL STEP — SET UP YOUR DOCUMENT

📋 HOW YOUR SONNET WILL BE SCORED
Your teacher looks at four things. Read this before you polish: it tells you exactly what a strong submission does.
Criterion Strong Developing Beginning
Form Fourteen lines of natural-sounding iambic pentameter; the full ABAB CDCD EFEF GG scheme with genuine rhymes; any metrical variation is deliberate and named in the craft statement. The frame is present, but several lines force their stress or a rhyme feels reached for; one section of the scheme wobbles. Module 1 — Justice in Greek Tragedy: Electra by Sophocles

This module asks one question in many forms: What does it mean to be truly honorable, and what does it reveal about us when we fall short? The poem sets a trap for its hero and for its reader. quizzes.title: Module 4 Intro
quizzes.description:
Module 4 — Love, Time, and the Sonnet: Shakespeare's Sonnets 18, 29, 116, and 130

For three weeks you will live inside the most famous fourteen-line room in English. This module asks one question in many forms: What can fourteen lines hold? What does a sonnet reveal about love, time, and human dignity? You will read four of Shakespeare's sonnets from the inside, then write, perform, and defend one of your own.

A note on your texts: Students must obtain lawful access to assigned literary works separately. Optima course materials are original instructional materials designed to support analysis, discussion, and assessment of the work. Copyrighted text, images, audio, or other protected materials are not reproduced in Canvas, VR, videos, downloadable files, or teacher resources except where expressly licensed, in the public domain, or approved as a limited fair-use excerpt for instructional analysis. All four sonnets in this module are in the public domain: the full texts are embedded free in your lessons, and the complete 1609 collection is free at Project Gutenberg (Shakespeare's Sonnets, eBook #1041). You do not need to buy anything for this module.

What do you expect a short, strict poem can reveal about love, time, and human dignity that a long free one cannot?* Write 3–4 sentences. There is no wrong answer yet — this is your starting point, and you will answer this question again at the end of the module.

Your module project is an **original Shakespearean sonnet** on a subject of your choice, with a craft statement and a recorded performance. What subject are you most drawn to right now? A person, a place, a fear, a season, a question — anything. One or two sentences; you are not committed to it yet.

This module asks you to read four sonnets closely (18, 29, 116, 130), keep your Module Organizer, write an **original sonnet** with a craft statement and recorded performance as the module project, and recite **one memorized sonnet** for the semester's Recitation Showcase. discussions.title: Discussion - Is the Revenge Just?
discussions.html:
Is the revenge just?

By the end of Electra, Electra and Orestes have taken their revenge, and the Chorus declares that "freedom is won." But throughout the play, characters disagree about whether that revenge is just — Clytaemnestra claims Justice as her own ally, and Chrysothemis warns that "Justice is sometimes dangerous."

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. State your position clearly: was Electra and Orestes' revenge just, unjust, or something in between?

2. Cite one specific moment from the public-domain text (classics.mit.edu/Sophocles/electra.html) — name the speaker and the moment, and quote a short line.

3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your position.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or who used different evidence than you did. Push the conversation forward — add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: this discussion is a good place to test the position you will defend in your essay. It is fine to change your mind here.

discussions.title: Week 1 Discussion
discussions.html:
What does the Green Knight's challenge reveal about Arthurian values?

The Green Knight rides into the most honored court in the world and dares anyone there to accept a deadly game. For a long moment, no one moves. Then Arthur seizes the axe, and Gawain steps in to take his place. The whole scene puts Camelot's honor on public display, and tests it.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. State your idea clearly: what does this scene reveal about what Arthur's court values most (for example, courage, reputation, courtesy, keeping one's word)?

2. Cite one specific moment from Fitt I of the public-domain text (Weston translation at the Camelot Project) — name the moment and quote a short line.

3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your idea.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who named a different value, or who used different evidence than you did. Push the conversation forward — add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: this discussion is a good place to test the thinking you will use in your disputatio essay, "Is Gawain a man of honor?" It is fine to change your mind here.

discussions.title: Discussion 2.2 - What Does the Pentangle Demand of Gawain?
discussions.html:
What does the pentangle demand of Gawain? Is it a realistic standard?

In Fitt II, the Pearl Poet paints the pentangle on Gawain's shield: five virtues (generosity, fellowship, purity, courtesy, and compassion), tied in an "endless knot" that must be kept whole, with none of the five ever dropped. It is a beautiful ideal. It may also be an impossible one.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. In your own words, explain what the pentangle demands of Gawain. What is the "endless knot" asking him to be?

2. Take a position: is this a realistic standard for a real person to keep? Say clearly yes, no, or partly.

3. Support your position with one specific detail from Fitt II (for example, a virtue from the pentangle, a moment on the winter journey, or the exchange-of-winnings game). Name the moment and, if you quote, keep it short and use the public-domain text: Weston translation.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position from yours. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: your answer here is a first test of the essay question you will argue later in the module, "Is Gawain a man of honor?" It is fine to change your mind as you keep reading.

discussions.title: Week 3 Discussion - Why the Parallel Structure?
discussions.html:
Why does the poet structure the hunt and temptation scenes in parallel?

Across Fitt III, the Pearl Poet keeps cutting between two spaces: Lord Bertilak hunting in the field (deer, then boar, then fox) and Lady Bertilak visiting Gawain's chamber. In Lesson 3.03 you saw that the two run in matching shapes, and that on the third day, when the lord hunts the cunning fox, Gawain himself turns cunning and hides the green girdle.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. State a clear answer: what does the parallel structure do for the reader? (For example: it invites comparison, builds suspense, or comments on Gawain's character.)

2. Point to one specific moment where the hunt and the temptation line up or contrast. Name the day and what happens in both spaces. You can find the text on the Week 3 Module Map (Weston translation, public domain).

3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your answer.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who gave a different answer, or who used a different day than you did. Add something: a new reason, a question, or a moment they did not mention. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: this is a good place to test the reading you will use in your essay's argument about Gawain's honor. It is fine to change your mind here.

discussions.title: Week 4 Discussion - Coward and Liar?
discussions.html:
Gawain calls himself a coward and a liar. Is he right?

At the Green Chapel, Gawain survives with only a nick on his neck. Bertilak (the Green Knight) tells him he is nearly faultless: he failed only a little, and only out of love for his own life. Back at Camelot, the whole court laughs, comforts him, and agrees to wear a green band in his honor. But Gawain does not accept any of this. He throws down the girdle, curses it, and condemns himself for cowardice (fear for his life) and covetousness (keeping the girdle), calling himself false.

So who has judged Gawain correctly?

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. State your position clearly: is Gawain right to call himself a coward and a liar, or is he being too hard on himself?

2. Cite one specific moment from Fitt IV in the public-domain text (Weston, 1898) — name the moment (for example, the guide's offer, the third blow, or the confession) and quote a short line.

3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your position. It is fair to weigh Gawain's verdict against Bertilak's or the court's.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or who used different evidence than you did. Push the conversation forward — add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: this discussion is a good place to test the position you are drafting in your essay (Project Feeder 4). It is fine to change your mind here.

discussions.title: Discussion - Does the Poem Celebrate or Expose?
discussions.html:
Does the poem celebrate Gawain's virtue, or expose its limits?

By the end of the poem, Gawain has kept the pentangle's promise for almost the entire test and failed just once, hiding the green girdle to save his life. Bertilak calls him the finest of knights and faults him only "a little." Gawain calls himself a coward. The court laughs and turns his badge of shame into a badge of honor. So which is the poem finally doing: holding Gawain up as an exemplar of chivalry, or quietly showing us the limits of that ideal when a real life is on the line?

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. State your position clearly: does the poem mainly celebrate Gawain's virtue, mainly expose its limits, or do something in between?

2. Cite one specific moment from the poem (the pentangle passage, Bertilak's verdict, Gawain's self-blame, or the court's response are all strong choices). Name the moment and quote a short line from your own copy or the public-domain text: the Camelot Project, University of Rochester.

3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment supports your position.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or who used different evidence than you did. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Be courteous: disagree with the idea, not the person. A good reply often begins with a concession (granting what they get right) before pushing back.

Note: this discussion is a good place to test the verdict you will defend in your disputatio essay. It is fine to change your mind here.

discussions.title: Discussion Post 1
discussions.html:
The irony in a portrait

Chaucer's narrator sounds impressed by nearly every pilgrim he describes. But a careful reader watches the details, because a detail can quietly contradict the compliment it sits inside.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. Choose one portrait from the General Prologue (the Knight, the Prioress, the Wife of Bath, the Miller, or the Pardoner).

2. Identify one detail that, on close reading, might be ironic rather than straightforwardly complimentary. Quote the specific line from the public-domain Middle English text (gutenberg.org/ebooks/2383); you may add the modern meaning in parentheses after the quotation.

3. Explain what the line says on the surface — and argue what it might mean beneath.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): do you agree with their reading of the irony, or do you see that detail differently? Push the conversation forward — add a reason, raise a question, or point to another detail in the same portrait. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: the pilgrim you argue about here could become the pilgrim of your module essay. This is a good place to test the reading before you commit to it.

discussions.title: Discussion Post 2
discussions.html:
The Miller's Insistence

The Host tries to keep the storytelling in order of rank: after the Knight, he invites the Monk. But the Miller, so drunk he can barely sit his horse, breaks in and insists on telling his tale immediately, announcing that he will "quyte the Knightes tale" (pay it back). The Host tells him to wait ("abyd, Robin, my leve brother, / Som bettre man shal telle us first another"), and the Miller refuses: he will speak now or leave the company.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. Answer the question: what does this insistence reveal about the Miller's character?

2. Cite one specific detail from the General Prologue's portrait of the Miller (his build, his wart, his bagpipes, his talent for stealing corn — whatever you find telling) and one moment from his Prologue or Tale. You can quote short Middle English lines from the public-domain text (Canterbury Tales, ed. Skeat — The Milleres Tale, Wikisource/Miller); also Project Gutenberg #2383).

3. Explain in a sentence or two how each detail supports your reading of him.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): does their reading of the Miller's character match yours, or do you see him differently? Push the conversation forward — add a reason, raise a question, or point to a detail they did not consider. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: this discussion is a rehearsal for your module essay, The Pilgrim's Portrait. If you are considering the Miller as your pilgrim, this is the place to test your reading of him.

discussions.title: Discussion Post 3 - Chanticleer
discussions.html:
What is Chaucer arguing about learning, pride, and self-deception?

Chaucer gives Chanticleer, a rooster, speeches full of classical learning, Latin quotations, and elaborate rhetoric. Chanticleer even wins his debate with Pertelote, proving from learned authorities that his dream is a true warning — and then a fox tricks him with flattery anyway.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. State your answer clearly: what is Chaucer arguing about learning, pride, and self-deception with this tale?

2. Cite at least two specific details from the tale in the public-domain Middle English text (The Canterbury Tales, Project Gutenberg #2383) — for example, a moment from the dream debate, the fox's flattery speech, the eyes-shut song, or the counter-trick. Name each moment precisely; a short quoted phrase is welcome but not required.

3. Explain in a sentence or two how those details support your reading.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): do you find Chaucer's argument convincing? Respond to someone whose reading differs from yours, or who used different evidence. Push the conversation forward — add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: the flaw you name here is good practice for your Pilgrim's Portrait essay, which makes the same kind of claim about a pilgrim and a virtue.

discussions.title: Discussion Post 4 - Sincere or Self-Serving?
discussions.html:
Sincere, or self-serving?

The central question of the Wife's tale is "What do women most desire?" The answer given is sovereignty — the power to make their own choices: "Wommen desyren to have sovereyntee / As wel over hir housbond as hir love." And the tale rewards the knight the moment he yields it.

But the teller of this tale spent her whole Prologue boasting about winning exactly that power from five husbands. So: is the Wife's tale a sincere argument for sovereignty, or is it self-serving — a story rigged to prove its teller right? (You may argue a middle position, but you must define it and defend it, not just say "both.")

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. State your position clearly: sincere, self-serving, or a defined middle position.

2. Cite one specific moment from the Prologue and one from the Tale (gutenberg.org/ebooks/2383) — name the moment and quote a short phrase (Middle English with your own gloss is welcome).

3. Explain in a sentence or two how each moment supports your reading.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who read the Wife differently than you did. Push the conversation forward — add a reason, raise a question, or point to a moment they did not consider (the gentilesse speech and the tale's ending are both underused). Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: this discussion is direct practice for Quick Write 4 and for your Pilgrim's Portrait essay. It is fine to change your mind here.

discussions.title: Discussion - Which Pilgrim Most Reveals Their Soul?
discussions.html:
Which pilgrim most reveals their soul through their tale?

Chaucer gives every pilgrim two portraits: the one the narrator paints in the General Prologue, and the one they paint of themselves the moment they open their mouths. The Knight tells a high romance that fits him like armor. The Miller barges in with a fabliau that suits him just as well. The Nun's Priest hides a sermon on pride inside a barnyard comedy. The Wife of Bath argues her own case for a hundred lines before her tale even starts. And the Pardoner confesses his fraud, then preaches a true sermon anyway. The module has asked one question all along: what does the character of a traveler reveal about their soul? Here is your chance to answer it for the company as a whole.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. Name the one pilgrim whose tale (or prologue-plus-tale) reveals the most about who they really are. You may choose your Module Project pilgrim or a different one.

2. Cite one specific moment where the telling gives the teller away: a detail the pilgrim did not have to include, a moral that fits them too well or not at all, or a gap between what they say and what they show. Quote a short line from your reading, or name the moment precisely.

3. Explain in a sentence or two how that moment reveals the soul behind the voice: does the tale display a virtue, betray one, or both at once?

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who chose a different pilgrim. Either name the piece of their evidence you find most convincing and add to it, or raise the strongest fair objection to their reading and see if they can meet it. Be courteous: disagree with the idea, not the person. A strong reply often begins by granting what the other reading gets right.

Note: this discussion is a good rehearsal for your Pilgrim's Portrait essay. If a classmate's objection exposes a weak spot in your thesis, that is a gift; fix it before you submit the final.

discussions.title: Discussion 4.1
discussions.html:
What does Sonnet 18 really praise: the beloved, or the poem itself?

Sonnet 18 opens by asking whether to compare the beloved to a summer's day, then spends eight lines proving the comparison fails. When the turn comes at line 9, the thing that saves the beloved from time is not beauty, luck, or nature. It is "this": the poem you are reading. Some readers find that a supreme act of love; others notice the poet never describes the beloved at all, and that the loudest praise in the poem is for the poet's own "eternal lines."

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. Take a position: is Sonnet 18 finally a poem about the beloved, or a poem about poetry? (You may argue it is genuinely both, but say how the two fit together.)

2. Quote one specific line from Sonnet 18 (the full text is on your Lesson 1.01 page) and name where it sits in the argument: which quatrain, or the couplet.

3. Explain in a sentence or two how that line supports your position.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or used different evidence. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a line they did not consider. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: this discussion is a rehearsal for your module project. By Week 3 you will write your own sonnet plus a craft statement explaining what your fourteen lines are really doing. Deciding what Shakespeare's are really doing is the best possible practice.

discussions.title: Discussion 4.2
discussions.html:
Is Sonnet 130 mostly a mockery, or the truest love poem in the sequence?

For twelve lines, Sonnet 130 refuses every compliment the love-poetry tradition taught readers to expect: her eyes are "nothing like the sun," coral is redder than her lips, music is "far more pleasing" than her voice. Then the couplet swears, "by heaven," that this love is "as rare / As any she belied with false compare." Some readers hear a brilliant joke aimed at a worn-out convention, a piece of literary criticism wearing a love poem's clothes. Others hear the most sincere declaration in all 154 sonnets, precisely because it refuses to flatter. The two readings pull against each other: a joke and a vow are different speech acts, and the poem seems to want to be both.

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. Take a position: is Sonnet 130 finally mockery of a convention, or a genuine love poem, or genuinely both? If you argue both, explain how the mockery and the sincerity depend on each other.

2. Quote one specific line from Sonnet 130 (the full text is on your Lesson 2.02 page) and name where it sits: which quatrain, or the couplet.

3. Explain in a sentence or two how that line supports your position. If your line is one of the refusals (lines 1–12), address what the couplet does to it.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who took a different position, or used different evidence. Add a reason, raise a question, or point to a line they did not consider. Be courteous; disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: this discussion is a rehearsal for your module project. On Friday you draft your own first quatrain, and you will have to make the same choice Shakespeare made: flatter your subject, or tell the truth about it. Arguing about his choice is the best possible practice for making yours.

discussions.title: Discussion - Which Sonnet's Definition of Love Holds Up Best?
discussions.html:
Which sonnet's definition of love holds up best?

Four sonnets, four different claims about love. Sonnet 18 promises that love (and poetry) can preserve what time destroys. Sonnet 29 shows love as a rescue: one thought of the beloved outweighs every misery. Sonnet 116 defines love as the fixed star that never alters, holding to the edge of doom. Sonnet 130 argues that honest love, without flattery, is rarer and truer than any exaggerated praise. They cannot all be the whole truth. Which sonnet's account of love holds up best against real human experience, the love you have actually seen in families, friendships, books, or history?

In your initial post (about 5–7 sentences):

1. Name your sonnet and state your position clearly: what does this poem claim about love, and why does that claim hold up best?

2. Cite lines: quote at least one line (or line-pair) from your chosen sonnet and name where it falls (for example, "the couplet," "the volta at line 9"). The full texts are in your lessons; every quotation must be a real line you can point to.

3. Test the claim against one specific example of real experience: something you have seen, read, or know from history. Explain in a sentence or two how the line and the example fit.

Then reply to at least one classmate (about 3–4 sentences): respond to someone who chose a different sonnet than you did. Grant what their sonnet gets right before you push back, then give one reason your sonnet's definition survives a test that theirs does not, or concede a case their sonnet handles better. Be courteous: disagree with the idea, not the person.

Note: this discussion is a good rehearsal for your craft statement. Defending Shakespeare's argument out loud makes it easier to defend your own.
